rules.title: Finite-dimensional vector-space convention

origin.tex:
From now on we will study only finite-dimensional vector spaces.
In the rest of this book we shall take `vector space' to mean 
`finite-dimensional vector space'.

rules.application: Carry the author's convention with material after this source passage; do not rewrite local hypotheses or apply it to earlier text. A source convention is not a claim that every object in a fragment is a vector space.

rules.title: Original complex-scalar convention

origin.tex:
This chapter requires that we factor polynomials.
But many polynomials do not factor over the real numbers;
for instance,
\( x^2+1 \) does not factor into a product of two linear polynomials
with real coefficients;
instead it requires complex numbers $x^2+1=(x-i)(x+i)$.

Consequently in this chapter 
we shall use complex numbers for our scalars,
including entries in vectors and matrices. 
That is, we shift from studying vector spaces over the real numbers
to vector spaces over the 
complex numbers.\index{complex numbers!vector space over}
Any real number is a complex number and
in this chapter most of the examples use
only real numbers but
nonetheless, the critical theorems require that the scalars be complex.
%</ReasonForShiftToComplexNumbers>

rules.application: The author switches the chapter to complex scalars. Explicit real-coefficient statements in the review remain real; a field convention never overrides a local hypothesis. rules.title: Original complex numbers and arithmetic

origin.tex:
While \( x^2+1 \) has no real roots and so doesn't factor over the real
numbers, if we imagine a root\Dash traditionally denoted \( i \), 
so that \( i^2+1=0 \)\Dash then \( x^2+1 \) factors into a product of linears,
\( (x-i)(x+i) \).
When we adjoin this root \( i \) to the reals and close the new system with
respect to addition and multiplication
then we have the 
complex numbers,\index{complex numbers}
\( \C=\set{a+bi\suchthat \text{$a,b\in\R$ and $i^2=-1$}} \).
%</ComplexNumbers>

For a scalar $z\in\C$, where $z=a+bi$,
we call $a$ the \definend{real part} of~$z$,
and~$b$ the \definend{imaginary part}.
We often picture complex numbers on the 
\definend{complex plane}\index{complex plane},
with $a$ plotted on the \definend{real axis}\index{real axis}, 
the horizontal axis, and $b$ plotted on the 
\definend{imaginary axis},\index{imaginary axis}
the vertical axis.
Note that the distance of the point from the origin is 
the length, $|a+bi|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$.

%<*ComplexOperations>
Recall the definitions of the complex number 
addition and scalar multiplication
\begin{equation*}
   (a+bi)\,+\,(c+di)=(a+c)+(b+d)i                  
  \qquad
  r\cdot(a+bi)=(ra)+(rb)i
\end{equation*}
(and consequently subtraction is $(a+bi)-(c+di)=(a-c)+(b-d)i$).
Recall also the definition of complex-complex multiplication.
\begin{align*}
     (a+bi)(c+di) &=ac+adi+bci+bd(-1)  \\
                  &=(ac-bd)+(ad+bc)i
\end{align*}
%</ComplexOperations>

rules.application: Retain the definitions of complex scalars, real and imaginary parts, absolute value and arithmetic. Preserve this source witness separately from exact unit bytes. No full prerequisite or proof-correctness certification is implied.

rules.title: Original factor and root definitions

origin.tex:
If a divisor \( d(x) \) goes into a dividend \( p(x) \) evenly,
meaning that \( r(x) \) is the zero polynomial,
then \( d(x) \) is a called a factor\index{factor}\index{polynomial!factor} 
of \( p(x) \).
Any root\index{root}\index{polynomial!root} of the 
factor, any \( \lambda\in\Re \) such that
\( d(\lambda)=0 \), is a root of \( p(x) \) since
\( p(\lambda)=d(\lambda)\cdot q(\lambda)=0 \).
%</PolynomialFactor>

rules.application: Retain the original explicit real-root example and the zero-remainder definition. Preserve this source witness separately from exact unit bytes. No full prerequisite or proof-correctness certification is implied.

rules.title: Complete statement for local proof 2

origin.tex:
\begin{corollary}  \label{co:RootOfPolyIsAssocLinearFactor}
%<*co:RootOfPolyIsAssocLinearFactor>
If \( \lambda \) is a root of the polynomial \( p(x) \)
then \( x-\lambda \) divides \( p(x) \) evenly, that is, 
$x-\lambda$ is a factor of $p(x)$.
%</co:RootOfPolyIsAssocLinearFactor>
\end{corollary}

rules.title: Complete local remainder proof used by the factor proof

origin.tex:
\begin{proof}
%<*pf:PolyDividedByLinearPolyIsConstant>
The remainder must be a constant polynomial
because it is of degree less than the divisor \( x-\lambda \).
To determine the constant, take the theorem's divisor
$d(x)$ to be $x-\lambda$ and 
substitute \( \lambda\/ \) for $x$. 
%</pf:PolyDividedByLinearPolyIsConstant>
\end{proof}

rules.title: Complete real factorization statement used by uniqueness examples

origin.tex:
\begin{corollary}  \label{co:RealPolysFactorIntoLinearsAndQuads}
%<*co:RealPolysFactorIntoLinearsAndQuads>
Any polynomial with real coefficients factors into a product of linear and
irreducible quadratic polynomials with real coefficients.
That factorization is unique; any two factorizations have the same factors
raised to the same powers.
%</co:RealPolysFactorIntoLinearsAndQuads>
\end{corollary}

rules.title: Earlier degree-n-or-less polynomial-space definition

origin.tex:
In general we write
\( \polyspace_n \) for the
vector space of polynomials of degree~$n$ or less 
\( \set{a_0+a_1x+a_2x^2+\cdots+a_nx^n\suchthat a_0,\ldots,a_n\in\Re} \),
under the operations of the usual polynomial addition and scalar 
multiplication.

rules.application: This earlier real-coefficient definition supplies the degree bound, not the coefficient field: this chapter changes coefficients to complex numbers. Keep JC1-SOURCE-003 separately. Preserve this source witness separately from exact unit bytes. No full prerequisite or proof-correctness certification is implied.

editorial_notes.text: Read this factorization statement for a nonzero polynomial with its leading scalar retained. Uniqueness requires normalized (monic) factors and ignores factor order; arbitrary nonzero rescalings of factors are otherwise possible. The zero polynomial does not have such a unique factorization. This is a separate qualification, not a silent change to the source.
